extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students, and readers of philosophy/science-method (geologists, astronomers, general scientific inquirers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for forming, evaluating, and applying scientific hypotheses, empirical laws, and causal inferences (including progressive effects and limits of induction). Targets reasoning used in geology, astronomy, physics, and general scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate inference from observed effects to past causes (geology/judicial analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is legitimate, in conformity with known laws, to conjecture what former collocations of known agents may have given birth to individual facts still in existence; this is the scope of geological inquiries and is no more illogical than judicial inferences from circumstantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from deposits resembling water-deposits or cooled igneous matter we may conclude such origins; if effects are larger than now produced, infer greater intensity of causes or enormously long times. Such inferences proceed from observed effects to past causes based on known laws and actual experience of origin, and should avoid introducing unknown agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish invention of new agencies from inductive conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great difference between inventing agencies to account for classes of phenomena, and endeavoring, in conformity with known laws, to conjecture what former collocations of known agents may have produced observed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor the latter (conjecturing past arrangements of known agents) when it rests on uniformities ascertained by induction; be wary of speculative hypotheses that posit unknown substances or unknown properties without necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat speculative suppositions as probable conjectures, not proved truths
rubrics_metrics.description: When a supposition introduces unobserved intermediaries (e.g., an intervening medium or ether) it should be regarded, at best, as a probable conjecture and not as a proved truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a speculative mechanism can account for phenomena (e.g., ether motions accounting for gravitation), that only shows it may be true, not that no other mode can be the true one. Maintain epistemic humility about such hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of known laws to reason about past states is legitimate but limited by assumptions about law-uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning backward from present effects to past causes by using known laws (as in Laplace's nebular hypothesis) is legitimate reasoning from a present effect to a possible past cause according to known laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, such reasoning assumes the existing laws of nature have remained the same over the long period in question; this assumption may be more hazardous the further back in time one infers, making such theories weaker in evidential support than closer-range geological inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive effects result from the continued action of a cause (composition of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause which continues in action should be analyzed as a succession of causes acting in succession; the progressive effect is the sum of the effects which such successive causes would produce if acting singly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: continual rusting of iron is the accumulated action of many particles of air acting successively; continued gravity produces progressive increases of motion. This justifies modeling such phenomena as summed successive contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate cause is the immediately preceding state, not the original remote cause
rubrics_metrics.description: When an effect is a continuous series (e.g., motion), the proximate cause of the state at any instant is the immediately preceding state (previous motion), not the original instantaneous impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if motion is retarded by a resisting medium, subsequent motion follows the retarded velocity; analyses of current motion should reference the immediate prior state rather than the distant original cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases of continual addition are amenable to deductive/mathematical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: When the continuance of a cause influences the effect only by adding to its quantity according to a fixed law (equal quantities in equal times), the result is computable by mathematical (deductive) methods; these are precisely the cases for differential calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions about the cumulative effect of continual causes should be treated deductively; experimental treatment of such infinitesimal compositions is often impractical or chimerical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for progressive change in the cause as well as for its continuance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a permanent cause also undergoes progressive change in circumstances that affect its effect, then the accumulated effect will change both from accumulation and from the changing action of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: seasonal temperature changes arise from both the continued action of the sun and its progressive change in diurnal position; models must include both accumulation and variation in cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize feedback: effects can react on causes and alter future behavior (periodicity vs divergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes may be altered by the effects they produce, so that the effect at one instant, becoming a cause, reacts upon the original causes and modifies subsequent effects; this interaction can produce periodical behavior or, in other ratios, non-periodic trajectories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: planetary motion periodicity arises because reactions of motion on the forces restore prior relations; different initial proportions could yield non-returning paths (parabola/hyperbola). Consider mutual interactions when predicting long-term behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of empirical law: observed uniformity without known explanatory derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws are uniformities shown by observation or experiment to exist, but which are not yet accounted for by known laws—they are derivative laws whose derivation is not yet known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include local tidal laws, certain weather sequences, anomalies to thermal expansion, biological breeding improvements by crossing, and various chemical/physical regularities. Treat these as provisional until resolved deductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit empirical laws to observed limits of time, place, and circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws can only be regarded as true within the limits of time, place, and circumstances in which they have been observed; they should not be safely extended beyond those limits without trial or explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the proposition that coal-beds rest on certain strata may hold on Earth but cannot safely be extended to the moon; if an empirical law depends on collocations of agents, those collocations may not hold elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement alone cannot establish causes—treat resultant generalizations as empirical
rubrics_metrics.description: When the only proof for a generalization is the Method of Agreement, it amounts to no more than an empirical law, because that method only identifies common circumstances, not which of them are true causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ascend beyond empirical status and establish causation one must use the Method of Difference (experimentation) or provide a deductive explanation (account for the 'why'). Results from Method of Agreement alone remain provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess authority of empirical laws by whether they likely reduce to laws alone or to laws plus collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws differ in strength: those likely resolvable into laws alone have greater authority than those likely dependent on particular collocations of agents in time/place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: developmental sequences in organisms likely derive from common causes (stronger empirical law), whereas geological superposition laws likely depend on particular historical collocations (weaker authority). Use such assessment when weighing generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative laws often depend on co-existence (collocation) as well as on laws; collocations are not law-like
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws are generated from ultimate laws together with an ultimate fact: the mode of co-existence (collocation) of some component elements. Collocations themselves show no perceivable uniform principle and cannot be reduced to laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus a regularity in effects may be produced by lawful action of agents arranged in an arbitrary collocation (kaleidoscope analogy). Be cautious inferring uniformities to other collocations or contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse invariable antecedent/sequence with causation (unconditional antecedent is the cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform succession of phenomena does not imply that successive terms are cause and effect; only the unconditional invariable antecedent is properly called the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: spring and summer are successive effects of solar heating; we should not call spring the cause of summer. In progressive growth (seedling to tree), the seedling and tree are terms in a series whose true first cause may be different; avoid misattributing causation to intermediate stages.
